note: Source says the love 'more especially' concerned with the good; qualifier dropped.
replacement: And the love, more especially, that is concerned with the good, and is perfected in company with temperance and justice, whether among gods or men, has the greatest power. It is the source of all our happiness and harmony, and it makes us friends with the gods above us and with one another. I suppose I too have left out several things that might be said in praise of Love, but I did not do so on purpose. And you, Aristophanes, may now fill the gap or take some other line of praise, for I see that you are rid of your hiccough.

note: Source has capital 'the God' (singular), which the style note says to keep as served.
replacement: And if we are not obedient to the gods, there is a danger that we shall be split up again and go about in basso-relievo, like the profile figures with only half a nose that are carved on monuments, and that we shall be like tallies. So let us urge all men to piety, that we may avoid evil and obtain the good, of which Love is to us the lord and minister. Let no one oppose him. Whoever opposes him is the enemy of the gods. For if we are friends of the God and at peace with him, we shall find our own true loves, which rarely happens in this world at present. I am serious, and so I must beg Eryximachus not to make fun of this or to see in it any allusion to Pausanias and Agathon, who, I suspect, are both of the manly nature and belong to the class I have been describing. But my words have a wider application. They include men and women everywhere. I believe that if our loves were perfectly fulfilled, and each of us, returning to his primeval nature, had his original true love, then our race would be happy. And if this would be best of all, then the next best thing, under present circumstances, must be the nearest approach to such a union, and that is to find a congenial love.

note: 'ungraceful' used as a noun subject; should be 'ungracefulness'.
replacement: Here is an excellent proof of her tenderness: she walks not on what is hard but on what is soft. Let us offer a similar proof of the tenderness of Love. He walks not on the earth, nor yet on the skulls of men, which are not so very soft, but in the hearts and souls of both gods and men, which are the softest of all things. In them he walks, and dwells, and makes his home. Not in every soul without exception, for where there is hardness he departs, and where there is softness there he dwells. And since he nestles always, with his feet and in every way, in the softest of soft places, how can he be anything but the softest of all things? Truly he is the tenderest as well as the youngest, and he is also supple in form. If he were hard and could not bend, he could not enfold all things, or wind his way unnoticed into and out of every human soul. A proof of his suppleness and fine proportion is his grace, which everyone admits to be in a special way the attribute of Love, for ungracefulness and love are always at war with one another. The beauty of his complexion is shown by his dwelling among the flowers. For he does not dwell among beauties, of body or soul or anything else, that are bloomless or fading, but in the place of flowers and scents; there he sits and stays. Of the beauty of the god I have said enough, and yet much more remains that I might say.

note: Source prints 'from the Love of the beautiful' with capital L; candidate lowercased it.
replacement: At his touch everyone becomes a poet, even if he had no music in him before (A fragment of the Sthenoaoea of Euripides.). This too is a proof that Love is a good poet and accomplished in all the fine arts, for no one can give to another what he does not have himself, or teach what he does not know. Who will deny that the creation of the animals is his doing? Are they not all the works of his wisdom, born and begotten of him? And as for the artists, do we not know that only the one whom love inspires has the light of fame? The one whom Love does not touch walks in darkness. The arts of medicine, archery and divination were discovered by Apollo, guided by love and desire, so that he too is a disciple of Love. The melody of the Muses, the metalwork of Hephaestus, the weaving of Athene, and the rule of Zeus over gods and men are also all due to Love, who was their inventor. So Love set the empire of the gods in order, the love of beauty, as is evident, for with deformity Love has no concern. In the days of old, as I said at the start, dreadful deeds were done among the gods, for they were ruled by Necessity. But now, since the birth of Love, and from the Love of the beautiful, every good has sprung up in heaven and earth. Therefore, Phaedrus, I say that Love is the most beautiful and best in himself, and the cause of what is most beautiful and best in all other things.
